definition: To be likely to do something.
example: She tends to eat healthy food every day.
note: German and Italian were missing the little linking word that the Spanish and French both have. Added so all four are complete.

definition: Belonging to them.
example: The red car is theirs, not ours.
note: German 'ihre' was the wrong form for this sentence. Changed to 'ihres', which is what you say for 'it is theirs'.

definition: In or from the west.
example: Western Europe includes France and Spain.
note: The definition said 'in or from the west' but the example was about cowboy films, and the German translation was the name of that film type. Example rewritten and Spanish and German changed so all four mean 'in or from the west'.

definition: Happening in all parts of the world.
example: The internet provides instant worldwide communication.
note: Italian was a three-word phrase while the others were single describing words. Changed to 'mondiale'.

definition: A secret romantic relationship.
example: He had an affair with his colleague at work.
note: Italian 'tresca' is an old-fashioned, disapproving word. The normal word today is 'relazione'.

definition: To come nearer to something.
example: The car began to approach the traffic light slowly.
note: Italian 'approcciarsi' is clumsy and mostly business jargon. The everyday word is 'avvicinarsi', which also matches the Spanish.

definition: Suitable or right for a particular situation.
example: Please wear appropriate clothes for the job interview.
note: Had been pushed onto the rare meaning 'to take something that is not yours'. The original German and French were both the describing word meaning 'suitable', which is the first meaning of 'appropriate'. Fully rebuilt around that.

definition: Feeling bad because you did something wrong.
example: He felt ashamed after he lied to his friend.
note: Italian 'vergognato' is not really used on its own. 'Mortificato' is the natural single word for feeling ashamed.

definition: To hit something again and again.
example: The drummer will beat the drum loudly.
note: Italian 'colpire' means to strike once. The definition is about hitting again and again, which is 'battere'.

definition: To choose actors for a play or film.
example: They will cast the main actor next week.
note: Spanish 'elegir' is the same word already used for 'elect', so the two entries clashed. Changed to 'seleccionar'.

definition: The leader of a group of people.
example: The chief of the tribe made an important decision.
note: German 'Häuptling' is only used for a tribal chief, while the other three are general. Changed to 'Anführer' so all four match the definition.

definition: The people who work together on a ship or plane.
example: The airplane crew prepared for takeoff.
note: Italian was a three-word phrase while the others were single words. Changed to 'equipaggio'.

definition: To remove someone from their job.
example: The company dismissed three workers last month.
note: The definition said 'to tell people they can leave' but Spanish and German both meant 'to fire someone from a job', and French was a loose phrase. All four now teach the job meaning, which is the first meaning of 'dismiss', and the example matches.

definition: Old, especially of people.
example: The elderly woman walked slowly with a cane.
note: German 'ältere' carried a grammar ending that did not fit on its own. Changed to the plain form 'älter'.

definition: Flat and smooth, with no bumps.
example: The road surface was even, with no bumps or holes.
note: Spanish 'parejo' is mainly Latin American. 'Liso' is understood everywhere and means smooth.

definition: To work out or understand something.
example: Can you figure out the answer to the maths problem?
note: Spanish 'descifrar' means to decode a secret message and French 'trouver' just means 'to find'. Both changed so all four mean working something out.

definition: A folder or holder for keeping papers together.
example: Please put the documents in the correct file.
note: Same word appears twice in the list with different Spanish. Spanish 'archivo' usually means a computer file; changed to 'carpeta' so the two entries agree.

definition: Bending cloth or paper so one part covers another.
example: She was folding the clean laundry and putting it away.
note: The four languages were in two different shapes. They now all use the same '-ing' form.

definition: A group of criminals who work together.
example: The police arrested a gang of thieves.
note: Spanish, German and French all meant a criminal group, but the definition and example described a group of school friends, and Italian 'comitiva' meant a group of friends going out. The first meaning of 'gang' is the criminal group, so the definition, example and Italian were all brought into line.

definition: To deal with a person or situation.
example: She can handle the difficult customers.
note: Italian 'maneggiare' is about handling an object with your hands. For dealing with people the word is 'gestire'.
